text.title: Incident Decision Template Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every incident decision record MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The record MUST be written and committed while the incident bridge is still open, within 2 minutes of the decision being spoken. A record written after the bridge closed MUST carry an `inputs[]` entry `reconstructed: true` with the reconstruction time; it is never presented as contemporaneous.

rationale.source: PagerDuty Incident Response documentation (Scribe role); Google SRE Book ch. 14 'Managing Incidents'

rule.rationale: Voice decisions evaporate. Ten minutes after the bridge, three engineers remember three different rollback thresholds, and the postmortem reconstructs a timeline from Slack scroll-back. The scribe writes while the commander talks; that is the whole point of the 2-minute form.

rule.statement: `inputs[]` MUST contain an entry named `options_considered` listing at least two options, one of which is "do nothing / keep observing". Each option is one line: action plus the reason it was or was not chosen.

rationale.source: Nygard, 'Documenting Architecture Decisions' (2011); MADR decision-record format ('Considered Options')

rule.rationale: A record with one option is a log line, not a decision. Listing the rejected option, including waiting, is what lets the postmortem judge whether the call was reasonable with the information available at the time, rather than with hindsight.

rule.statement: `inputs[]` MUST contain an entry named `blast_radius` naming the affected systems, regions or tenants and a number: percent of traffic, request count, customer count or revenue per minute. "Some users" and "part of the platform" are rejected.

rationale.source: Google SRE Book ch. 14 'Managing Incidents'; widely established incident-severity practice

rule.rationale: Blast radius decides who gets paged, whether the status page updates and whether legal is told. A decision to restart the primary database looks different at 3% of read traffic than at 100% of checkout. Without the number the severity is whatever the loudest voice on the bridge says it is.

rule.statement: `inputs[]` MUST contain an entry named `rollback_trigger` with a metric name, a threshold, a time window and the rollback command or runbook URL (e.g. "checkout 5xx rate above 2% for 5 consecutive minutes on dashboard X; rollback: `helm rollback checkout 41`"). "If it gets worse" is rejected.

rationale.source: Google SRE Workbook ch. 16 'Canarying Releases'; Google SRE Book ch. 22 'Addressing Cascading Failures'

rule.rationale: The moment a mitigation makes things worse is the moment nobody wants to admit it. A pre-agreed numeric trigger removes the argument: the metric crossed the line, the runbook runs. Without it the bridge spends twenty minutes debating whether the new graph is noise.

rule.statement: `decision` MUST be a single imperative sentence naming the action, the target system and when it takes effect ("Disable the recommendations sidecar in eu-west-1 now"). Sentences containing "consider", "maybe", "look into" or "should probably" are rejected.

rationale.source: Widely established incident-communication practice; content/04-procedure.xml step 4

rule.rationale: A hedged decision is executed differently by each engineer who reads it. During an incident the record is read by people who were not on the call and are about to type a command; ambiguity here is a second incident.

rule.statement: `owner` MUST be the incident commander or the person the commander explicitly delegated the call to, in `role:handle` form. The engineer who executes the change is recorded in `inputs[]` as `executor` when different. A record whose owner is a team, a channel or the executor without delegation is rejected.

rationale.source: PagerDuty Incident Response documentation (Incident Commander role); Incident Command System

rule.rationale: Incidents fail when two people believe they are making the call. Recording the commander as owner is the one governance rule this artefact needs: it makes the delegation chain visible and stops "I thought you approved that" in the postmortem.

rule.statement: Every `evidence[]` URL MUST resolve to a timestamped signal from this incident: a dashboard link with the time range pinned, an alert, a log query, a chat-message permalink or a commit. At least one URL MUST show the state of the system at the moment of the decision. Links to general documentation do not count as evidence.

rationale.source: Google SRE Book ch. 15 'Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure'

rule.rationale: The postmortem needs to answer "what did they see when they decided". A dashboard link without a pinned time range shows tomorrow's healthy graph, and a docs page proves nothing about that night. Pinned evidence makes the decision reviewable rather than defensible only by memory.

rule.statement: `review.next_review_at` MUST be no later than the incident's postmortem date, and the review outcome MUST state whether the rollback trigger fired and whether the measured blast radius matched the recorded one. An incident record still unreviewed after the postmortem is closed is marked stale.

rationale.source: Google SRE Book ch. 15 'Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure'; content/02-output-contract.xml `review` block

rule.rationale: The record only earns its keep if someone checks whether the call was right. Reviewing it at the postmortem, when the timeline is on the table, costs minutes; reviewing it a quarter later costs an archaeology session and produces nothing the team will act on.
